title: Pure equity vs asset allocation: how the two approaches differ
summary: Pure equity or a mix of equity and debt? See fall size, recovery time, effort and tax compared, with a worked ₹8,00,000 example from dated NIFTY 50 history.
body_markdown:
Pure equity means all your invested money sits in shares, for example through equity funds. Asset allocation spreads the money across equity and other kinds of investment, such as debt.


Equity means shares of companies. Debt means loans to governments, banks or companies, in the form of bonds and similar paper.


## What is the difference between pure equity and asset allocation?


Pure equity puts every rupee you have invested into shares, while asset allocation splits the money between kinds of investment. Asset allocation is how your money is split between asset classes, kinds of investment that each behave in their own way, such as equity and debt. The full idea is in[how asset allocation impacts your portfolio](https://koshex.com/blog/how-asset-allocation-impacts-your-portfolio) .


Here is how the two compare on the points that change:


All in equity A mix of equity and debt


What moves the value Share prices Share prices for the equity part, interest rates for the debt part


How big a fall can be The NIFTY 50, an index of 50 large companies' shares, fell 59.9% between 8 January and 27 October 2008 The same fall hits only the equity share of the money


Riskometer For example, every listed flexi cap fund read Very High on 29 September 2026 Each fund carries its own label, so a mix of funds shows more than one


Effort Nothing to bring back into line between asset classes The split drifts as prices move and needs bringing back


Tax when you move money A switch between funds is a sale of the old units Topping up one part by switching from the other is a sale; new money avoids one


What you give up The smaller falls a mix would have taken Some of the rise in a long climb


The riskometer is the risk label SEBI makes every fund show, on six levels from Low to Very High. A fully invested equity portfolio scores no lower than High and usually Very High.


Debt is not free of risk either. SEBI's investor website notes that bond prices may fall when interest rates rise, and may rise when rates fall.


## How big are the falls in each?


If the rest of the money holds steady, the loss on the whole holding is roughly the fall in equity multiplied by the share in equity.


Take a made-up ₹8,00,000, not a suggested mix. Put all of it in equity, or ₹5,00,000 in equity and ₹3,00,000 in debt. Now run both through the NIFTY 50's fall from 12,362.30 on 14 January 2020 to 7,610.25 on 23 March 2020. An index is a list of companies picked by fixed rules, whose combined value is tracked every day. The NIFTY 50 figures here are the index price alone, without dividends.


For the debt part, use the NIFTY 10 yr Benchmark G-Sec index. It is an index of government bonds, not a fund, and its figure includes interest. Over those same weeks it rose from 1,857.72 to 1,918.50, about 3%.


- **All in equity:** ₹8,00,000 became ₹4,92,481, a fall of 38.4%.
- **The mix:** the equity part became ₹3,07,801 and the debt part ₹3,09,815. Together that is ₹6,17,616, a fall of 22.8%.


Costs and tax are left out of both lines.


The 2008 fall was larger. The NIFTY 50 closed at 6,287.85 on 8 January 2008 and 2,524.20 on 27 October 2008, down 59.9%. The example's government-bond figures cover 2020 only, so there is no mix figure for 2008.


## How long does each take to recover?


An all-equity holding recovers only when the market does, and in the two dated cases that took months to years. It was 5 November 2010, about 2 years and 10 months later, before the NIFTY 50 closed above its 8 January 2008 level again.


After 14 January 2020 it took about 10 months, to 9 November 2020. These are past dates, not a pattern.


A mix begins its climb from a smaller hole. In the example above, left alone from 14 January to 9 November 2020, the ₹8,00,000 all in equity was worth ₹8,06,390. The mix was worth ₹8,30,223. That used the NIFTY 50 at 12,461.05 and the government-bond index at 2,020.14.


Treat it as one window, not a pattern. It shows a mix can end ahead after a fall and a recovery. It does not show that it usually does.


## Which approach is harder to stick with?


The harder one is whichever has falls you cannot watch without selling. Selling is what turns a paper loss into a real one.


Go back to the example. The all-equity holding showed ₹4,92,481 against ₹8,00,000 invested. Would you have held on at that figure? The mix showed ₹6,17,616 on the same day, still a heavy loss but a different one to sit through.


AMFI is direct about the risk. Investors "should not invest in the equity schemes unless they can afford to take the risk of possible loss of principal." Principal is the money you put in. For how to judge your own limit, read[what risk tolerance is](https://koshex.com/blog/what-is-risk-tolerance-and-why-is-it-important) . If you are already looking at a fall,[should I redeem my funds since the markets are down](https://koshex.com/blog/should-i-redeem-my-funds-since-the-markets-are-down) goes through the decision. Koshex talks you through sharp market falls before you redeem.


## How much work and tax does each involve?


Pure equity needs no bringing back into line between asset classes, while a mix drifts and needs attention, and each switch is a sale for tax. In the example, the mix's equity share fell from 62.5% to 49.8% after the March 2020 fall. That is rebalancing: bringing your mix back to the split you chose after markets have moved it.


Some investors rebalance when an asset class has moved about 5 percentage points from its target. Others check once or twice a year. Neither is a SEBI or AMFI rule. Rebalancing is about keeping risk where you set it. It does not promise a higher return, and in a long rising market, selling some of the rising asset each time can leave you with less than if you had left it alone. The method is in[how to rebalance your mutual fund portfolio](https://koshex.com/blog/how-to-rebalance-your-mutual-fund-portfolio) .


For tax, a switch is a sale of the old units and a purchase of new ones, and the new units' holding period, how long you have owned a unit, starts on the switch date. The Income-tax Act counts a transfer as including "the sale, exchange or relinquishment of the asset". The rules below apply to any gain:


- **Equity-oriented fund** (at least 65% in equity shares of domestic listed companies): a gain on units held 12 months or less is short-term and taxed at 20%. A long-term gain, on units held more than 12 months, is taxed at 12.5% on the amount above ₹1,25,000 in the tax year.
- **Specified Mutual Fund** (more than 65% in debt and money market instruments), units bought on or after 1 April 2023: the gain is short-term whatever the holding period. It is taxed at your slab rate, the rate for your income band.
- **Cess:** a 4% Health and Education Cess is added to the tax.


You get the ₹1,25,000 allowance once per tax year, not once per fund. Gains from all your equity funds, and from any shares you sell, share it.


An exit load, a fee some funds charge if you sell within a set time, may also apply. Koshex customers can switch between schemes of the same fund house on Koshex. A hybrid fund holds both equity and debt in one fund. Its own trading, including its rebalancing inside the fund, is not taxed in your hands. See[how to switch mutual fund schemes](https://koshex.com/blog/how-to-switch-mutual-fund-schemes) for the steps.


## Who does each approach tend to suit?


It depends on conditions rather than on which approach is better. What matters is how far away the goal is, whether you might need the money early, how your finances could absorb a fall, and how you behaved in past falls.


A long time to the goal, money you will not need early and a record of sitting through falls make all-equity easier to hold. A goal within a few years, uncertain income or a habit of selling in falls point towards holding some debt.


On horizon, Koshex suggests five years or more for large cap funds. A large cap fund must keep at least 80% in the 100 biggest companies. There is no ratio that is right for everyone.[How asset allocation impacts your portfolio](https://koshex.com/blog/how-asset-allocation-impacts-your-portfolio) explains what decides a mix.


Time also changes the picture. As a goal comes closer, there is less time for a fall to recover before you need the money. This is why some investors move money from equity towards debt in the last few years before a goal, and why SEBI's life cycle funds reduce their equity share as the target date nears.[Is it the right time to switch from equity to debt](https://koshex.com/blog/is-it-the-right-time-to-switch-from-equity-to-debt) covers that move.


## What do the long-run numbers say?


AMFI's illustration rates are the mean of 10-year rolling returns from 1 June 2014 to 31 May 2024. Equity comes out higher: 12.42% for the Nifty 50, against 6.61% for the CRISIL 10 year Gilt Index and 7.85% for the CRISIL Composite Bond Index.


These are past averages, not a forecast. Set beside those averages, the NIFTY 50 fell 59.9% in 2008 and 38.4% in early 2020.
